newsitem.title: UK: UK tells Nigeria to reform or face sanctions.
newsitem.headline: UK tells Nigeria to reform or face sanctions.

text.p: New Foreign Secretary Robin Cook vowed on Monday that human rights would dominate British foreign policy and said sanctions should be imposed on Nigeria if it failed to make democratic reforms.

"The new Labour government will put human rights at the heart of our foreign policy," he told a news conference called to announce his ministry's priorities in the wake of Labour's landslide election win on May 1.

When in opposition, Labour took a stronger line than the Conservative government over the failure of Nigeria's military government to introduce long-delayed democratic reforms and over its alleged human rights abuses.
Labour consistently supported tough sanctions against the oil-rich west African state and Cook indicated that little would change now it was in power.
"I believe the world should keep up strong economic pressure and must be prepared to apply sanctions until Nigeria returns to the democratic fold," he said.
Cook had earlier told BBC radio that sanctions should be applied in a way that started to restore democratic rights to the people of Nigeria.
But the Commonwealth and other major trading nations are divided over whether and how to punish Nigeria, saying sanctions could be counterproductive.

Tony Lloyd, Britain's new minister responsible for Africa, called on the Commonwealth to put as much pressure as possible on Nigeria in the run-up to a heads of government meeting in Edinburgh this October.
"What we're praying for is the Commonwealth to use its influence to make a difference," Lloyd told reporters afterwards.

Cook laid out his priorities in a "mission statement" which said the government would push for regulation of the international arms trade to ensure weapons were not sold "for external aggression or internal repression".
Britain, as one of the world's four leading defence exporters, would seek responsible international regulation of the arms trade through an eight-point plan.
"We want a European Union code of conduct to ensure that if we don't take up (an arms) contract, our other partners don't take it up either," he said.
Cook said his main goals were ensuring Britain's security, making best use of overseas posts to boost trade, working with other nations to fight crime and spreading the values of human rights.
Cook launched a high-profile charm offensive last week with trips to Paris and Bonn to underscore Britain's determination to end years of antagonism between the EU and the Conservatives.
He denied the emphasis on fence-mending would harm ties with the United States, saying Washington would be less interested in a Britain marginalised at the edge of Europe.
Over the next 12 months, Britain would focus on making a success of its European Union presidency in the first half of next year and on enlarging NATO to bring in three new member states, he said.

The blunt-spoken Cook makes little secret of his desire to shake up the staid Foreign Office and this was reflected in the way his news conference was staged in the huge and highly ornate Locarno room.

A large screen had been erected at one end of the room and the massed ranks of the media had to sit through a five-minute video highlighting Britain's strengths, complete with thumping rock music, before Cook appeared.
